A Sno-Cat straddling a crevasse during the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition. 1957

The 1955–58 Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition was a Commonwealth-sponsored private expedition that successfully completed the first overland crossing of Antarctica, via the South Pole. It was headed by British explorer Dr. Vivian Fuchs, with New Zealander Sir Edmund Hillary leading the New Zealand Support team.

Fuchs set out from one side of the continent and Hillary was to lay a path to the Pole from the other. Fuchs set out November 1957, with a twelve-man team travelling in six vehicles; three Sno-Cats, two Weasels and one specially adapted Muskeg tractor. On route, the team were also tasked with carrying out scientific research including seismic soundings and gravimetric readings.

It was not originally intended that Hillary would travel as far as the South Pole, but when he had completed laying supply depots he saw the opportunity to beat the British, he continued south, reaching the Pole on January 3, 1958. Hillary's party was just the third (preceded by Amundsen in 1911 and Scott in 1912) to reach the Pole overland. Hillary's arrival also marked the first time that land vehicles had ever reached the Pole.

Fuchs' team reached the Pole on 19 January 1958, then continued overland, following the route that Hillary had laid, while Hillary flew back to Scott Base. The party finally arrived at Scott Base on March 2, 1958.

The entire Fuchs' expedition covered 3,473 km (2,158 miles) of previously unexplored snow and ice in 99 days.
